result:
I was thinking about how quiet the world gets at 5:47 a.m.

Not the dramatic quiet of movies. The real one. The radiator ticks once and then stops. The refrigerator hums down a notch. Outside, the streetlights are still on but they look embarrassed about it, like they forgot to turn off. A bus sighs by and the whole building shivers.

I make coffee the way my grandfather taught me without ever teaching me. Fill the kettle, wait for it to sing, then pour too fast and apologize to the grounds. I drink it standing at the sink because the kitchen table feels too formal for mornings. The steam fogs up the window and for a few seconds I can draw in it with my finger. A small cloud, a line, a terrible doodle of a cat. Then it fades.

People think freedom is big. Travel, change jobs, move to the coast. But most of the freedom I actually use is small and stupid and repeatable. Choosing to write a sentence even when it’s bad. Choosing to leave the blinds open. Choosing to notice the way the light hits the chipped blue mug on the third shelf.

The pigeon on the fire escape has been there for three days. He watches me like I’m on a reality show. This morning he tilted his head and I swear he was judging my coffee technique. I waved. He didn’t wave back. Fair.

I like that the day doesn’t need me to be interesting. It just needs me to be here long enough for it to happen to me. The light gets warmer. The steam clears. The pigeon leaves.

And that’s enough to start with.
